title: Bioengineered Chewing Gum Cuts Oral HPV by 93% in Cancer Study
excerpt: Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania have developed a bean-derived chewing gum that dramatically reduced levels of HPV and cancer-linked bacteria in oral samples from head and neck cancer patients, while leaving beneficial bacteria intact.
body:
• A bioengineered chewing gum made from lablab beans reduced HPV levels by 93% in saliva and 80% in oral rinse samples from head and neck cancer patients.
  • When enhanced with an antimicrobial peptide called protegrin-1, the gum also brought two cancer-linked bacteria to near-undetectable levels in a single dose.
  • Unlike radiation therapy, the gum selectively targeted harmful microbes while preserving beneficial oral bacteria.
  • The ex vivo study, published in Scientific Reports, was led by University of Pennsylvania researchers and funded by the NIH and the National Cancer Institute.

A Gum That Targets Cancer-Linked Microbes

Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania School of Dental Medicine have developed a bioengineered chewing gum that can dramatically reduce levels of three microbes linked to head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) — one of the most common and aggressive cancers affecting the mouth and throat.

The study, published in Scientific Reports in February 2026, found that extracts from the gum reduced human papillomavirus (HPV) levels by 93% in saliva samples and by 80% in oral rinse samples from patients with HNSCC.

When the gum was further enhanced with protegrin-1, an antimicrobial peptide that targets harmful bacteria, a single dose brought levels of two cancer-associated bacteria — Porphyromonas gingivalis and Fusobacterium nucleatum — to near zero. The reductions exceeded 99% in ex vivo samples.

How It Works

The gum is derived from lablab beans and contains a naturally antiviral protein called FRIL (Flt3 receptor-interacting lectin). FRIL binds to viral glycoproteins on the surface of HPV, aggregating the virus and reducing its ability to enter host cells.

"The global increase in oropharyngeal cancer is linked to HPV infection. And Pg and Fn infections worsen survival rates of untreated recurrent or metastatic oral cancer, even after surgery and risk-adjusted adjuvant therapies."

— Henry Daniell, lead researcher, University of Pennsylvania

The protegrin-1 component extends the gum's reach to anaerobic bacteria. Together, the two active ingredients provide broad coverage against three known cancer drivers while preserving the commensal streptococcal species that form part of a healthy oral microbiome.

This selectivity distinguishes the approach from radiation therapy, which can reduce beneficial bacteria while increasing levels of disease-causing yeast like Candida albicans.

Why It Matters

Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma was the seventh most common cancer type worldwide among adolescents, young adults, and middle-aged adults in 2022, according to the researchers. HPV-driven oropharyngeal cancer has been rising globally, and the bacteria P. gingivalis and F. nucleatum have been linked to tumor-promoting inflammation, immune suppression, and resistance to treatment.

Despite recent advances in oncology, many newly approved therapies have not significantly improved five-year survival rates or quality of life for HNSCC patients, the researchers noted. That gap has driven interest in complementary strategies that target the microbial drivers of the disease.

What Comes Next

The study was an ex vivo clinical study — meaning the gum extracts were tested on patient samples in a laboratory setting, not administered to patients directly. The researchers are now looking to advance to full clinical trials.

"Our findings support the value of advancing these therapies to clinical trials as adjuvants with current treatments or as prophylaxis to prevent infection and transmission."

— Henry Daniell, University of Pennsylvania

If the gum proves effective in clinical settings, it could serve as either a low-cost adjunct to existing cancer treatments or as a preventive measure for people at risk of HPV-related oral cancers. The chewing gum format would make it accessible and easy to use, requiring no specialized medical infrastructure.

The research was conducted across multiple institutions including UCLA and the University of Kansas Medical Center, with funding from the National Institutes of Health and the National Cancer Institute.
